verses.translation_literal: Why are [the] nations in uproar, and [the] peoples mutter emptiness?
verses.translation_dramatic: Why? Listen to them: the nations seethe like a sea against a wall, and the peoples, in a thousand tongues, mutter their plans into the dark. What is it all for? A rumble of voices, a great noise, and nothing inside it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens not with a statement but with a gasp: Why? Whoever speaks is watching a crowd boil and cannot believe it. Play it as astonishment, not lecture. In the ancient Near East a new king's accession was exactly the moment vassals tested him: tribute stopped, coalitions formed, armies gathered. Rashi and Radak tie the scene to 2 Samuel 5:17, when the Philistines marched up as soon as David was anointed king over all Israel.

The KJV's 'heathen' is a later, Christian-sounding word; the Hebrew is simply goyim, 'nations', and le'ummim, 'peoples', two near-synonyms (Metzudat Zion, Ibn Ezra). 'Imagine a vain thing' is also soft. The verb yehgu is the same one used for the quiet murmur of a man who 'meditates' on Torah in Psalm 1:2, sounding out words under his breath. Here it is the opposite: they murmur riq, 'emptiness', 'nothing at all'. Hear the echo of Psalm 1, which many ancient teachers counted as one psalm with this one (Radak, Meiri): the righteous murmur Torah; the nations murmur void. The verb ragshu occurs only here; its sound, with the sibilants of ragSHU, is the hiss of a crowd.

philological_notes.note: A rare verb for the roar of a gathered crowd, used only here. Radak and Metzudat Zion link it to the 'crowd' of evildoers in Psalm 64:3 and to the Aramaic Targum 'tumult' in Ezekiel 30:10.
The root means to murmur or mutter, and so to meditate; it is the verb of Psalm 1:2. Placed beside riq 'emptiness', it gives a mocking mirror of the righteous man's murmuring of Torah.
'Emptiness, nothing' (Metzudat Zion: a thing with no substance). Here an adverbial accusative: they plan to no effect.

verses.translation_literal: Kings of [the] earth take their stand, and rulers have conferred in council together, against YHWH and against his anointed.
verses.translation_dramatic: The kings of the earth plant their feet. The rulers draw close in a whispering circle, heads together, one will among them all, and the target is named at last: the LORD, and the one he has anointed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene moves from the noise of the street to the closed room. First the kings 'take their stand', a military-sounding verb: they present themselves like an army drawn up or a court in session. Then the rulers sit in a council whose very name, sod, means a secret meeting; the verb nosdu has the same root as 'counsel' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak). Radak adds that counsel is the 'foundation' of a deed, as a foundation is of a building, so there may be a faint pun on laying plans.

The target is double: YHWH and his 'anointed', meshicho. KJV and ASV capitalise nothing and add 'saying', pulling verse 3 forward; the Hebrew has no 'saying' (the quotation begins abruptly in v. 3). 'Anointed' means a king whose installation was marked by oil, not yet a title of a future redeemer; Radak points to Samuel's anointing of David. Rebelling against the Great King's chosen vassal is, in the ancient world's logic, rebelling against the king himself. Radak notes the Philistine lords are called 'kings' out of their own pride.

philological_notes.note: STEPBible takes it from יסד 'to found'; Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as 'took counsel' from סוד, a secret council. Passive-reflexive (Niphal): they conferred among themselves.
'His anointed one': the king consecrated with oil. The word is a title for kings and priests here, long before it names a future figure.

verses.translation_literal: Let us tear off their fetters, and let us throw from us their ropes!
verses.translation_dramatic: "Come, let us rip their fetters apart! Fling their ropes away from us!" The words are theirs now, loud and fierce, a shout that tries to sound like freedom.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the conspirators speak, and the voice changes to a hot, first-person plural. Actors should give it the swagger of a rebel slogan. The imagery is of a draft animal: mosrot are the leather straps that lash the yoke, 'avot are the thick, twisted ropes (Rashi, Metzudat Zion, Metzudat David). The rebels see their tribute and obedience as an ox's harness, and the line works like a political cartoon: the ones who hold the yoke are YHWH and his king.

The verse is also a classic Hebrew parallelism: the second line repeats the first with a synonym, 'for beauty of speech and strength' (Metzudat David, Radak). The KJV 'bands' and 'cords' keep this well, but 'break asunder' for nattequ and 'cast away' hide the violence: nattaq is to rip off, as one tears a seam or pulls a thing out of its socket. And the pronoun is 'their' (-mo, an archaic poetic form), not 'his': the rebels talk of both YHWH and the king as 'them'.

philological_notes.note: Straps tied to the yoke, a figure for the burden of obedience. The suffix -eimo is an archaic poetic 'their'.
Thick ropes of three twisted strands (Metzudat Zion); stronger than mosrot. Malbim takes the order as ascending strength.

verses.translation_literal: [The one] sitting in the heavens laughs; [the] Lord mocks at them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And above the noise, above the stars, someone sits, unhurried and enthroned, and he laughs. The Lord mocks them, quietly.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera lifts. After three verses of human thunder, the scene cuts to a throne in heaven and a sound that no one expected: laughter. 'Sitting' here means enthroned, at ease (Radak: 'sitting' for God is a figure of reign and permanence), so the contrast is between the crowd on its feet in a panic and the One who does not even rise. The two verbs are present, habitual: He laughs, He mocks (Rashi notes that they are verbs of the present, of continuing action; KJV 'shall laugh' and 'shall have them in derision' turns it into a future threat and loses the immediacy).

The KJV's 'have in derision' is the right sense, but a modern ear needs the plain word: la'ag is to jeer. Radak says this is a figure from human speech: God does not literally laugh, but the picture tells how little weight the rebellion has. Notice the change of divine title: from YHWH (v. 2) to Adonai, 'the Lord', the sovereign master. The title names the very lordship the rebels want to shake off.

philological_notes.note: 'He laughs.' Radak reads divine laughter as a figure of speech from human behaviour, comparing Psalm 59:9 and 37:13.
Archaic poetic form of 'to them'; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'at them'.

verses.translation_literal: Then he speaks to them in his anger, and in his fury he terrifies them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then he speaks. Not a shout, a single word in anger, and the heart of every conspirator goes cold. In his fury he sends them reeling.
verses.directors_commentary:
The laughter stops. 'Then' (az) is the hinge of the psalm: the moment the joke turns. God's speech is a weapon: his word and his wrath are the same event (Radak: 'his words with them are his anger and fury, which he sends upon them'). A director should take the pause between the laughing and the first syllable as long as possible.

The KJV's 'vex' is badly softened: yevahalemo is from bahal, to throw into panic, to terrify, the verb used of a people stampeded by sudden fear. 'Vex' now means to annoy. 'In his sore displeasure' is also pale beside harono, 'in his burning rage'. The first word, be'apo, literally 'in his nose', is the Hebrew idiom for anger: when furious one snorts and the nostrils flare. The earlier line also has the eilemo form, an archaic 'to them' (Ibn Ezra, Rashi); a few commentators read it as 'to their mighty ones' (Ibn Ezra rejects this; Radak calls it less likely).

philological_notes.note: Literally 'in his nose', the standard Hebrew idiom for anger, since the nostrils flare.
To terrify, to throw into panic; stronger than the KJV 'vex'.

verses.translation_literal: "And I, I have installed my king on Zion, mountain of my holiness."
verses.translation_dramatic: "But I," he says, "I have set my own king on Zion, on my holy mountain. It is already done."
verses.directors_commentary:
Here God speaks, and what he says is a flat fact, not an argument. The opening 'And I' (va'ani) is emphatic and contrasting: 'You are conspiring; I have already acted' (Metzudat Zion reads the vav as 'but'). The verb nasakhti is rare. STEPBible has 'installed', which fits the commentators: Ibn Ezra and Radak connect it with nesikhim, 'princes' (Joshua 13:21), a word of rank, so the sense is 'I have enthroned'. The common alternative, 'poured out' (as in a libation), is behind YLT's 'anointed' and fits the oil of the previous verses, but the rank sense is what the commentators prefer.

'My king' is both 'the king that is mine' and, grammatically, 'the one who is king under me' (Radak). The place is the key: Zion was a Jebusite stronghold until David took it (2 Samuel 5:7), and Radak notes the Philistines came up only after he did. 'Mountain of my holiness' is a closer rendering than the KJV's 'holy hill', because in Hebrew the mountain belongs to God's holiness, not merely a hill that happens to be sacred.

philological_notes.note: 'I have installed, set up as ruler'; connected by Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion to nesikhim 'princes'. The other root, 'pour', gives 'I have anointed'.
'My king.' Radak notes that the possessive suffix can mean 'the king who is mine' or 'who rules me', and compares Psalm 74:12.

verses.translation_literal: Let me recount concerning [the] decree of YHWH: he said to me, "My son [are] you; I, today, I have begotten you."
verses.translation_dramatic: Now the king himself speaks. "I will tell you the decree of the LORD. He said to me: You are my son. Today, this very day, I have become your father."
verses.directors_commentary:
A new voice: the king steps forward and reports what God said to him on the day of his enthronement. The word choq, 'decree', is a written, binding statute; Metzudat Zion links it to carving or inscribing. This is the court language of the ancient Near East: at the coronation the god-patron declares the king his 'son', and the Israelite version keeps the form while stripping out the myth. Radak and Meiri read it as adoption: the king is God's son as a servant is chosen and trusted, not a physical child. Compare 2 Samuel 7:14, 'I will be a father to him and he will be a son to me'.

Mind the tense: yelidtikha is 'I have begotten you', a completed act announced for the day, 'today'. KJV 'this day have I begotten thee' keeps the sense but its 'begotten' now sounds like a doctrine, where the Hebrew sounds like a court proclamation. BBE's 'given you being' is closer to the biological, which the commentators avoid. The word 'I' (ani) is emphasised: 'I, I myself, today.'

philological_notes.note: A decree or fixed statute, from the verb 'to cut, engrave'. Metzudat Zion links it to inscription.
'I have begotten you.' Read by Radak, Meiri and Rashi as the day the king is taken as son, comparing 'the Rock that begot you' (Deuteronomy 32:18) said of Israel as a whole.

verses.translation_literal: Ask of me, and I will give nations [as] your inheritance, and [as] your possession [the] ends of [the] earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Ask me. Only ask, and the nations are yours for an inheritance, and the farthest edges of the earth for your own."
verses.directors_commentary:
The speech of the decree continues, and it is startlingly generous: God offers, and the son has only to ask. The scene is a father to an heir (Ibn Ezra: it is the way of a father to settle an inheritance on his son). 'Inheritance' (nachalah) and 'possession' (achuzzah) are the legal words for family land that passes down and stays held; the language turns the whole world into the king's estate, which should be heard against the tiny real kingdom of Israel.

The KJV has 'the heathen' again for goyim; the Hebrew is simply 'nations'. 'Uttermost parts' is quaint for afsei eretz, 'the ends of the earth', which Ibn Ezra and Radak relate to efes, 'nothing, the last point'. Rashi adds that the 'asking' is prayer before every war. Radak sees it fulfilled in David's reported victories, citing 2 Samuel 8 and 1 Chronicles 14:17.

philological_notes.note: 'The ends of the earth,' where the land runs out; Ibn Ezra and Radak link it to efes, 'nothing, end', and to qets 'end'.

verses.translation_literal: You will break them with a rod of iron; like a potter's vessel you will smash them.
verses.translation_dramatic: "You will break them with a rod of iron. You will smash them like a potter's jar flung to the ground, and the pieces will fly."
verses.directors_commentary:
The offer carries a sword. The 'rod of iron' (shevet barzel) is a royal sceptre and a weapon at once: the word shevet means both a ruler's staff and a club, so the king's sign of office is his means of enforcing it. Iron was the metal of the new age, hard and hard to work; to carry an iron sceptre would be a boast in a world where bronze was the norm. Rashi even reads it as 'the sword'.

The second image is what ancient audiences would know: Egyptian execration texts wrote the names of enemy rulers on clay pots and ritually smashed them. The potter's jar, cheap and brittle, shatters into scraps that scatter (Radak and Metzudat Zion on tenapetsem: breaking together with scattering, as with the jars in Judges 7:19). The KJV 'dash them in pieces' is fair; but 'break' for tero'em hides a known ambiguity: with other vowels the same letters can mean 'you will shepherd them', as YLT's 'rule them' and BBE's 'ruled by you' reflect. The commentators here all read 'break' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak), and the parallel 'smash' agrees; but a listener who knows the shepherd's rod of Psalm 23 may hear the bitter overtone of a shepherd's rod made of iron.

philological_notes.note: 'You will break them'; Ibn Ezra and Radak gloss it as to shatter, citing Jeremiah 15:12 ('can iron be broken?'). The same consonants could be read from רעה, 'shepherd', which YLT and BBE follow.
To smash so that the fragments scatter; Radak and Metzudat Zion compare the jars shattered in Judges 7:19.

verses.translation_literal: And now, kings, show insight; take correction, judges of [the] earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: So now, you kings, grow wise. Take the lesson, you rulers of the earth, while there is still time to take it.
verses.directors_commentary:
'And now' (ve'attah) is the turn from report to warning: the speaker, having said what God has decreed, now turns to the audience in the room and addresses the rebels directly. In legal and prophetic rhetoric ve'attah introduces the consequence of what was just said. Radak imagines David speaking to the besieging kings.

The two commands are a pair that answers the rebels' cry. Hasqilu, 'show insight', is the verb of wisdom; hivvaseru, 'let yourselves be corrected', is from the root of musar, discipline, and so it echoes mosrot, the 'fetters' of verse 3 (Ibn Ezra notes that hivvaseru is the opposite of mosroteimo). They wanted to tear off the straps (musar); now they are told to accept the strap's lesson. 'Judges of the earth' (shofetei aretz) is Ibn Ezra's 'the rulers': in the ancient world a judge was one who governed, not only one who tried cases. The KJV 'Be wise now therefore' is acceptable but loses the bite of the Hebrew wordplay.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of yasar: 'be disciplined, accept correction.' Ibn Ezra sets it against mosroteimo in v. 3.
Judges, but in the sense of 'governors, rulers'; Ibn Ezra equates them with the 'rulers' of v. 2.

verses.translation_literal: Serve YHWH with fear, and rejoice with trembling.
verses.translation_dramatic: Serve the LORD, and let awe be in it. Rejoice, but with trembling.
verses.directors_commentary:
The warning becomes an order, and it is brief. 'Serve' ('ivdu) is the word for what a vassal does for his overlord and for what a worshipper does for God, so it answers the rebels' refusal in verse 3 directly: they threw off the yoke; they must now take on service. Ibn Ezra: it is the reverse of 'let us tear off'.

The paradox is on purpose. Gilu normally means joyful shouting and dancing; here it is paired with 'trembling', so the joy is that of those who have escaped the thing they feared (Rashi: you will rejoice if you serve, when the trembling that seizes the godless comes, Isaiah 33:14; Metzudat David: the trembling falls on the rebels, not on you). Radak: rejoice that this is the will of God. The BBE rewrites the verse as 'kissing his feet and giving him honour', an invention that borrows from the next verse; the Hebrew has only fear and trembling. A director should find a tone that carries both at once, awe that is not despair.

philological_notes.note: 'And rejoice,' with a note of exultation. Ibn Ezra mentions an opinion that the form is an imperative with the force of a blessing or permission.

verses.translation_literal: Kiss [the] son, lest he be angry and you perish [on the] way, for it flares in a moment, his anger. Blessed [are] all [who] take refuge in him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Kiss the son in homage, before his anger breaks and you are lost on the road, for his wrath can kindle in an instant. But happy, happy are all who take refuge in him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last verse is the hardest in the psalm, and an honest director tells the actors why. 'Kiss' is clear: kissing the hand, foot or hem was how a vassal sealed homage (Ibn Ezra, Radak). The object, bar, is the problem. In Hebrew 'son' is ben; bar is the Aramaic word for 'son', which appears nowhere else in the psalter, in a text whose verse 7 has already used ben. Radak weighs three options: 'the son' (bar as ben), 'the pure' (as in bar levav, 'pure of heart', Psalm 73:1), or 'the chosen' (as in beru lakhem ish, 'choose you a man', 1 Samuel 17:8, in the sense of 'Saul the chosen of the LORD'). Meiri prefers a rendering about purity: 'arm yourselves with purity', a pun on nashaq 'to kiss' and neshek 'weapon'. The KJV, ASV and Webster translate 'the son'; YLT chooses 'the Chosen One'; BBE drops the clause. I keep 'son' because verse 7 has prepared it and the royal setting makes homage to the king the natural reading.

The KJV 'perish from the way' misleads: the Hebrew has no 'from'; derekh is an accusative of the road or course, 'you perish [on] the way', as Psalm 1:6 says that 'the way of the wicked will perish' (Rashi, Radak). The versions split on kim'at. Rashi takes it as 'in a brief moment': the anger flares suddenly, and I follow him in the literal layer. Metzudat David, the KJV and YLT take 'even a little': if his anger burns only slightly, you are already lost. Both are possible; the first makes the warning more urgent and gives the closing blessing a sharper contrast. The psalm ends where Psalm 1 began, with 'ashrei, 'blessed', a frame that holds the two poems together.

philological_notes.note: Aramaic 'son', or 'pure' (as in bar levav), or 'chosen'. The commentators divide: Radak lists all three, Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David take 'pure', Meiri prefers purity, Ibn Ezra takes 'son' and compares Proverbs 31:2. Verse 7 has ben.
'You perish [on the] way.' Ibn Ezra and Radak read derekh as an accusative of respect: they perish through their way, as in Psalm 1:6.
'In a moment' (Rashi: in a brief moment, suddenly) or 'even a little' (Metzudat David: when his anger burns to a small degree).
